sections.title: Core Foundations & Conceptual Framework
sections.content:
• **All-India Federation Principle**: Proposed a federation comprising British Indian Provinces and Princely States, though it never materialized due to optional entry clauses for princely states.
• **Abolition and Introduction of Dyarchy**: Dyarchy was abolished at the provincial level and introduced at the central (federal) level, though federal dyarchy never actually came into operation.
• **Bicameralism at the Centre**: Out of 11 provinces, 6 (Madras, Bombay, Bengal, United Provinces, Bihar, and Assam) were introduced to bicameral legislatures (Legislative Council and Legislative Assembly).
• **Key Metric / Factor**: Extended franchise significantly, granting voting rights to roughly 14% of the British Indian population based on property, tax, and educational qualifications.

items.definition: Abolition of diarchy in provinces; provinces were recognized as autonomous units of administration within their defined spheres, directly responsible to popular ministers.
Established in Delhi in 1937 under the Act, serving as an intermediate court of appeal between high courts and the Privy Council in London, with original jurisdiction in inter-provincial disputes.

Furthered the divide-and-rule policy by extending separate electorates not just to Muslims, but also to Depressed Classes (Scheduled Castes), Women, and Labor.

items.title: Major Geographical Distribution / Regional Hubs
items.content:
• **Bicameral Provinces**: Centered in major administrative hubs like Bengal, Bombay, Madras, United Provinces, Bihar, and Assam.
• **Separation of Burma and Aden**: Burma was officially separated from India, and Aden was made a Crown colony, reshaping imperial administrative boundaries in the East.

items.title: Challenges, Reforms & Forward Strategy
items.content:
• **Bottlenecks / Issues**: Overriding discretionary powers of the Governor-General and Governors crippled provincial autonomy; princes rejected the federation.
• **Policy Interventions**: Led to the 1937 provincial elections, Congress ministry formations, and eventually formed the bedrock of independent India's constitutional draft.

items.title: Mnemonic for Federal Legislative Lists
items.content:
• **Memory Acronym / Phrase**: 'F-P-C: Fifty-Nine, Fifty-Four, Thirty-Six'
• **Decoded Meaning**: Federal List = 59 items, Provincial List = 54 items, Concurrent List = 36 items.
• **Prelims Exam Value**: Instantly verifies exact legislative item counts when trap options mix up numbers.

items.title: Retention Rule of Thumb
items.content: • **Core Formula / Rule**: Remember 'Provinces got Freedom (Autonomy), Centre got Diarchy (which never worked), and Burma got Separated' in 1935.

upscNotes.content: Examiner Trap: UPSC frequently states that 'Diarchy was introduced at the Centre AND Provinces under the 1935 Act.' This is false—diarchy was *abolished* in provinces and *introduced* at the Centre (though never implemented).

Mains Value Addition: Emphasize that while the 1935 Act has been criticized as a 'charter of slavery' by nationalist leaders, nearly 70% of the provisions of the present-day Indian Constitution are directly drawn from it due to its detailed administrative mechanics.

keyTakeaways: The Government of India Act 1935 laid the constitutional blueprint for federalism and provincial autonomy in pre-independence India.
It abolished provincial diarchy, introduced federal diarchy (unimplemented), and classified powers into Federal, Provincial, and Concurrent lists.
It served as the primary legal and structural template for the Constitution of Independent India.
